subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Why carbon can build so many different molecules
Condensation joins monomers into polymers
Hydrolysis splits polymers back into monomers
Starch and glycogen store energy compactly
Cellulose: straight chains bundled into a strong wall
Glycoproteins let cells recognize each other
Lipids are defined by what they dissolve in
Double bonds, melting point and where fats are stored
Adipose tissue: energy store and insulator
Phospholipids arrange themselves into bilayers
Steroids slip through the bilayer
The parts of any amino acid
Condensation makes dipeptides and longer chains
Which amino acids must come from food
Heat and pH change a protein's shape
R-groups give proteins their diversity (HL)
Sequence decides shape (HL)
Coils and pleats in the backbone (HL)
Where polar and non-polar amino acids sit (HL)
Proteins from several polypeptides (HL)

questions.q: Carbon forms an enormous diversity of compounds, on which life is based. Which statement about the bonding of a single carbon atom is correct?
options: It forms up to four covalent bonds, single or double, with carbon or other non-metal atoms
It forms any number of covalent bonds, which is why so many carbon compounds exist
It transfers its four outer electrons to other atoms, giving charged compounds
It links to neighbouring carbon atoms by weak hydrogen bonds that are easily broken
optionWhy: A carbon atom has four outer electrons, so it can form up to four covalent bonds, as four single bonds or a combination of single and double bonds, with other carbon atoms or with atoms of other non-metallic elements. Repeating this gives chains, branches and rings.

A student who merges "carbon forms many bonds" with "carbon forms many compounds" picks this. The maximum is four bonds per atom; the diversity comes from carbon atoms linking to each other repeatedly in chains and rings.
A student who models every bond on ionic bonding picks this. Carbon forms covalent bonds, sharing a pair of electrons with each partner atom, so its compounds are uncharged molecules.

A student who thinks of hydrogen bonds as the general bond of biology picks this. Carbon atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds; hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between molecules or parts of molecules.
questions.explain: A carbon atom has four outer electrons, so it can form up to four covalent bonds, as four single bonds or a combination of single and double bonds, with other carbon atoms or with atoms of other non-metallic elements. Repeating this gives chains, branches and rings.

questions.q: Two monosaccharides are joined by a condensation reaction to form a disaccharide. What happens in this reaction?
options: A molecule of water is taken in and split to supply the atoms that join the monomers
A hydrogen bond forms between the two monomers, holding them together as a disaccharide
Water dissolves the two monomers so that they meet, but no water is formed or used
A covalent bond forms between the monomers and a molecule of water is released
optionWhy: A student who has the two reactions swapped picks this. Water is used and split in hydrolysis, which breaks bonds; condensation forms a bond and releases water.
A student who thinks of hydrogen bonds as the bond of biology picks this. The bond formed by condensation is a strong covalent bond, which is why the disaccharide is stable until it is hydrolysed.
A student who sees water only as the solvent picks this. Water is a product of condensation: one molecule is released for every bond formed.

In a condensation reaction an -OH from one monomer and an -H from the other are removed and combine to form water, leaving a covalent (glycosidic) bond between the monomers. Repeated condensations build a polysaccharide.
questions.explain: In a condensation reaction an -OH from one monomer and an -H from the other are removed and combine to form water, leaving a covalent (glycosidic) bond between the monomers. Repeated condensations build a polysaccharide.

questions.q: Why is the digestion of a polymer into its monomers described as a hydrolysis reaction?
options: Water acts only as the solvent in which enzymes break the polymer into its monomers
Water molecules are split, and the -H and -OH produced are added to the monomers
Breaking the bonds between the monomers releases the energy that was stored in those bonds
Water molecules are released as each bond between neighbouring monomers is broken
optionWhy: A student who sees water as the inert medium picks this. Water is a reactant that is split and incorporated into the products, which is exactly what the name hydrolysis records.
Hydrolysis means splitting with water. For each bond broken, one water molecule is split; its -H is added to one product and its -OH to the other, so the water is incorporated into the monomers.
A student who believes bond-breaking releases energy picks this. Hydrolysis releases very little energy; the energy from food is released later, when monomers are oxidized in cell respiration.
A student who has swapped the two reactions picks this. Water is released in condensation, when bonds form; in hydrolysis water is used up as bonds break.
questions.explain: Hydrolysis means splitting with water. For each bond broken, one water molecule is split; its -H is added to one product and its -OH to the other, so the water is incorporated into the monomers.

questions.q: Liver cells store glucose in the form of glycogen. Why is the glucose not simply stored as free glucose?
options: Glycogen is relatively insoluble because of its size, so it does not affect the osmotic balance of the cell
Glycogen is insoluble because it is non-polar, so it stays separate from the watery cytoplasm
The branches of glycogen make its glucose hard to remove, so the store is not used up too quickly
Glycogen stores extra energy in the glycosidic bonds that link its glucose monomers together
optionWhy: Glycogen is a very large molecule and is relatively insoluble, so large amounts can be stored without raising the solute concentration of the cytoplasm. Free glucose is soluble and would draw water into the cell by osmosis.
A student who reuses the lipid explanation for insolubility picks this. Glycogen is covered in polar hydroxyl groups; it is relatively insoluble only because its molecules are so large.
A student who imagines branches as protection picks this. Branching does the opposite: it provides many chain ends at which glucose can be removed rapidly by hydrolysis.

A student who believes energy is stored in bonds picks this. Polymerizing glucose does not add energy; the energy is released when glucose is oxidized in cell respiration, and glycogen is simply a compact, osmotically inert way of holding it.
questions.explain: Glycogen is a very large molecule and is relatively insoluble, so large amounts can be stored without raising the solute concentration of the cytoplasm. Free glucose is soluble and would draw water into the cell by osmosis.

questions.q: Cellulose gives plant cell walls high tensile strength. Which feature of cellulose is responsible for this?
options: The glycosidic bonds within cellulose are very much stronger than those within starch
The chains coil into tight helices that stretch and recoil like a spring
Beta-glucose is a larger monomer than alpha-glucose, giving thicker chains
Straight chains lie side by side in bundles, cross-linked by many hydrogen bonds
optionWhy: A student who looks for strength in stronger covalent bonds picks this. The glycosidic bonds in cellulose and starch are both covalent and of similar strength; the difference lies in how the chains are arranged and cross-linked.
A student who transfers the coiled shape of amylose to cellulose picks this. Cellulose chains are straight, and it is their side-by-side bundling, not coiling, that gives strength.
A student who thinks the two forms of glucose differ in size or atoms picks this. Alpha- and beta-glucose have identical formulae; beta-glucose differs only in the orientation of the -OH on carbon 1.

The straight, unbranched chains of beta-glucose pack side by side and are grouped into bundles in which a very large number of hydrogen bonds link the chains. Although each hydrogen bond is weak, together they give the bundles great resistance to stretching.
questions.explain: The straight, unbranched chains of beta-glucose pack side by side and are grouped into bundles in which a very large number of hydrogen bonds link the chains. Although each hydrogen bond is weak, together they give the bundles great resistance to stretching.

questions.q: The ABO blood groups depend on glycoproteins on the surface of red blood cells. Which statement about these ABO antigens is correct?
options: The A and B antigens differ only in the sugar at the end of their carbohydrate chain
The A and B antigens are two entirely different proteins with unrelated amino acid sequences
Group O red blood cells carry a third antigen, the O antigen, in the place of the A or B
The carbohydrate part of each antigen projects inwards into the cell's cytoplasm
optionWhy: ABO antigens are glycoproteins with a shared base carbohydrate chain. The alleles of the ABO gene encode enzymes that add different terminal monosaccharides to that chain, producing the A or the B antigen, and it is this small difference in the carbohydrate that other cells and antibodies recognize.

A student who thinks of antigens only as proteins picks this. The identity of an ABO antigen lies in its carbohydrate chain, not its protein; A and B share the same base and differ in one terminal sugar.
A student who extends the A/B naming pattern to O picks this. Group O cells carry the unmodified base chain and neither the A nor the B antigen; there is no O antigen.

A student who has not registered the orientation of glycoproteins picks this. The carbohydrate faces outwards from the cell surface, which is what allows it to act in cell–cell recognition and to be met by antibodies.
questions.explain: ABO antigens are glycoproteins with a shared base carbohydrate chain. The alleles of the ABO gene encode enzymes that add different terminal monosaccharides to that chain, producing the A or the B antigen, and it is this small difference in the carbohydrate that other cells and antibodies recognize.

questions.q: A triglyceride is only sparingly soluble in water but dissolves readily in a non-polar solvent. What explains this?
options: Its molecules are too large to fit between water molecules, but a non-polar solvent has more room
Its molecules are mostly non-polar C–H bonds, with few groups that hydrogen-bond to water
Its molecules are less dense than water, so they float on the surface rather than dissolving
It is a polymer of fatty acids, and polymers such as starch do not dissolve in water either
optionWhy: A student who reuses the size explanation for polysaccharides picks this. A triglyceride is far smaller than a soluble protein; its insolubility in water comes from its non-polar nature, not its size.

Lipids are hydrophobic because they are non-polar. Water molecules hydrogen-bond to one another and exclude molecules that cannot join in, so a triglyceride is sparingly soluble in water; in a non-polar solvent, whose molecules interact by the same weak attractions, it dissolves readily.
A student who merges floating with not mixing picks this. Density decides whether a liquid floats, not whether it dissolves: ethanol is less dense than water yet mixes with it completely.

A student who classes triglycerides as polymers picks this. A triglyceride is one glycerol linked to three fatty acids, not a polymer, and its behaviour in solvents is explained by polarity, not by polymer size.
questions.explain: Lipids are hydrophobic because they are non-polar. Water molecules hydrogen-bond to one another and exclude molecules that cannot join in, so a triglyceride is sparingly soluble in water; in a non-polar solvent, whose molecules interact by the same weak attractions, it dissolves readily.

questions.q: Three fatty acids each have 18 carbon atoms in their chain. X has no C=C double bonds, Y has one and Z has three. Which has the lowest melting point, and why?
options: Z, because its C=C bonds kink the chain so that molecules pack less closely together
X, because C=C bonds are stronger than single bonds and hold Y and Z molecules together
Z, because it has the fewest hydrogen atoms and so the fewest bonds to break as it melts
X, because having no double bonds makes it the unsaturated one, and unsaturated fats melt lowest
optionWhy: Each C=C double bond puts a kink in the hydrocarbon chain. The kinked molecules of Z cannot pack closely, so the intermolecular attractions between them are weakest and less energy is needed to separate them: Z, the polyunsaturated fatty acid, melts at the lowest temperature.

A student who confuses bonds within molecules with attractions between molecules picks this. C=C bonds are within each molecule; what matters for melting is how closely the molecules pack, and straight saturated chains such as X pack most closely and melt highest.

A student who counts the bonds to be broken picks this. Melting breaks no covalent bonds; it overcomes the weak attractions between molecules. Z does melt lowest, but only because its kinked chains pack least closely, not because it contains fewer bonds.

A student who takes "saturated" to mean full of double bonds picks this. A fatty acid is saturated with hydrogen, not with double bonds: X, with no C=C, is the saturated one, and its straight chains pack most closely, so it melts highest, not lowest.
questions.explain: Each C=C double bond puts a kink in the hydrocarbon chain. The kinked molecules of Z cannot pack closely, so the intermolecular attractions between them are weakest and less energy is needed to separate them: Z, the polyunsaturated fatty acid, melts at the lowest temperature.

questions.q: Which property of triglycerides makes them well suited to long-term energy storage in adipose tissue?
options: They release less energy per gram than carbohydrates, so a store of them lasts longer
They are very large molecules, so they cannot dissolve and leave the adipose cell
They release about twice the energy per gram of carbohydrates when oxidized
Their many ester bonds store energy that is released when the bonds are broken
optionWhy: A student who thinks of carbohydrate as "the energy food" picks this. Triglycerides release about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates; a store lasts because it is large and compact, not because it is low in energy.

A student who explains lipid insolubility by size picks this. Triglycerides are insoluble because they are non-polar, not because they are large; a triglyceride is far smaller than a glycogen molecule.

Triglycerides yield roughly twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate, and they are stored without the water that accompanies glycogen and without osmotic effects, so a great deal of energy is held in a small, stable mass, which is what a long-term store needs.

A student who believes energy is stored in bonds picks this. Breaking ester bonds by hydrolysis releases very little energy; the large yield comes from oxidizing the fatty acids and glycerol in cell respiration.
questions.explain: Triglycerides yield roughly twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate, and they are stored without the water that accompanies glycogen and without osmotic effects, so a great deal of energy is held in a small, stable mass, which is what a long-term store needs.

questions.q: Phospholipids are shaken with water in a test tube, with no cells or enzymes present. What happens, and why?
options: Bilayers form, because the hydrophilic heads face the water and the hydrophobic tails face each other
Nothing organized forms, because phospholipid bilayers can only be built by enzymes inside living cells
Bilayers form, because covalent bonds link the fatty acid tails of neighbouring phospholipids
The phospholipids react with the water, because being amphipathic means acting as both an acid and a base
optionWhy: Phospholipids are amphipathic. In water the hydrophilic phosphate heads associate with water while the hydrophobic fatty acid tails are excluded from it, so the molecules spontaneously arrange themselves in a double layer with heads outwards and tails inwards; no enzymes are needed.

A student who assumes every biological structure is built by enzymes picks this. Bilayer formation is a consequence of the hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions of the molecule and happens spontaneously in water.

A student who expects an orderly structure to be covalently bonded picks this. No covalent bonds form between phospholipids; the bilayer is held by the exclusion of the tails from water, which leaves it fluid.

A student who confuses amphipathic with amphoteric picks this. Amphipathic means having a hydrophilic and a hydrophobic region, and it is this that drives bilayer formation; no acid–base reaction with water occurs.
questions.explain: Phospholipids are amphipathic. In water the hydrophilic phosphate heads associate with water while the hydrophobic fatty acid tails are excluded from it, so the molecules spontaneously arrange themselves in a double layer with heads outwards and tails inwards; no enzymes are needed.

questions.q: Testosterone binds to receptors inside its target cells. How does it get through the plasma membrane to reach them?
options: It is too large to pass between the phospholipids, so it is carried through a channel protein
It is a non-polar steroid, so it dissolves in the hydrophobic core of the bilayer and diffuses across
It is a protein hormone, so it is pulled into the cell after binding to a receptor on the surface
It is enclosed in a vesicle at the cell surface and taken into the cell by endocytosis
optionWhy: A student who applies the rule that only small molecules cross the bilayer picks this. Polarity matters more than size here: non-polar steroids dissolve in the bilayer itself and need no channel.

Testosterone is a steroid, a lipid built on four fused carbon rings, and is non-polar. It dissolves in the hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer and passes through by simple diffusion, which is why steroid hormones can act on receptors inside the cell.
A student who assumes all hormones are proteins picks this. Testosterone is a steroid lipid, not a protein; protein hormones cannot cross the bilayer, whereas steroids can.
A student who defaults to endocytosis for anything entering a cell picks this. A steroid needs no vesicle: being non-polar it diffuses straight through the hydrophobic core of the membrane.
questions.explain: Testosterone is a steroid, a lipid built on four fused carbon rings, and is non-polar. It dissolves in the hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer and passes through by simple diffusion, which is why steroid hormones can act on receptors inside the cell.

questions.q: Which feature is shared by all 20 of the amino acids that are coded for in the genetic code?
options: An amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and an R-group are all bonded to one alpha carbon atom.
The R-group is identical in every amino acid, and the amine and carboxyl groups are what vary.
The amine group is bonded directly to the carbon atom of the carboxyl group, with no carbon between.
The amine group is an NH₃ group, with the same structure as a molecule of ammonia.
optionWhy: This is the generalized structure of an amino acid: a central alpha carbon carrying the amine group, the carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and the R-group. Only the R-group differs between the 20 amino acids.

A student who takes the fully drawn groups to be the variable parts picks this. In fact it is the other way round: the amine group, carboxyl group and hydrogen are the same in every amino acid, and only the R-group differs.
A student who writes an amino acid as NH₂–COOH picks this. In fact both groups are attached to the alpha carbon, which sits between them and also carries a hydrogen and the R-group.

A student who carries ammonia's three hydrogens over to the amine group picks this. In fact one of the nitrogen's bonds is to the alpha carbon, so the amine group is –NH₂; it becomes –NH₃⁺ only when it binds a hydrogen ion.
questions.explain: This is the generalized structure of an amino acid: a central alpha carbon carrying the amine group, the carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and the R-group. Only the R-group differs between the 20 amino acids.

questions.q: Two amino acids react to form a dipeptide. Which statement describes this reaction?
options: A molecule of water is taken in to provide the atoms needed to link the two amino acids together.
The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amine group of the other, and water is released.
The R-group of one amino acid bonds to the R-group of the other, forming the peptide bond between them.
The amine group of one amino acid forms a hydrogen bond with the carboxyl group of the other, and no water is released.
optionWhy: A student who confuses condensation with hydrolysis picks this. In fact water is a product: a hydroxyl group from the carboxyl group and a hydrogen from the amine group are removed and combine to form the water that is released.

This is the condensation reaction: amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + water. The peptide bond forms between the carbon of the carboxyl group and the nitrogen of the amine group, and one molecule of water is released.

A student who assumes the distinctive R-groups must do the chemistry picks this. In fact the R-groups take no part in the reaction; the peptide bond is in the backbone, between a carboxyl group and an amine group.

A student who thinks the link between amino acids is a hydrogen bond picks this. In fact the peptide bond is a covalent C–N bond formed by a condensation reaction between the carboxyl group and the amine group, and one molecule of water is released as it forms.
questions.explain: This is the condensation reaction: amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + water. The peptide bond forms between the carbon of the carboxyl group and the nitrogen of the amine group, and one molecule of water is released.

questions.q: What is meant by an essential amino acid?
options: One that the body needs in larger quantities than the non-essential amino acids.
One of the 20 amino acids, all of which must be supplied by the protein in the diet.
One that is found in animal protein but is absent from all plant-based foods.
One that cannot be synthesized in the body and must be obtained from food.
optionWhy: A student who reads essential in its everyday sense of important picks this. In fact the term says nothing about quantity: an essential amino acid is one that cannot be synthesized in the body and so must be obtained from food.

A student who thinks every amino acid has to come from food picks this. In fact only the essential amino acids must come from food; the non-essential ones can be made in the body from other amino acids.

A student who believes plant proteins contain no essential amino acids picks this. In fact plant proteins contain essential amino acids, although a single plant protein may be low in one or more of them; the definition concerns the body's inability to make them.
This is the definition: essential amino acids cannot be synthesized and must be obtained from food, whereas non-essential amino acids can be made from other amino acids.
questions.explain: This is the definition: essential amino acids cannot be synthesized and must be obtained from food, whereas non-essential amino acids can be made from other amino acids.

questions.q: When egg white is heated, its soluble proteins turn into a white solid. What has happened to the protein molecules?
options: Heat has broken the peptide bonds, so the polypeptides have been split into amino acids.
Heat has killed the proteins, so they are no longer able to carry out their functions.
Heat has changed their shape temporarily, and they will refold as soon as the egg white cools.
Heat has broken the bonds holding their folded shape, so they have unfolded.
optionWhy: A student who thinks denaturation breaks the protein down picks this. In fact the covalent peptide bonds are unaffected by cooking temperatures; it is the weak bonds holding the folded shape that break, so the sequence is intact but the shape is lost.

A student who uses everyday language about heat killing things picks this. In fact proteins are molecules and cannot be killed; they have been denatured, meaning their conformation has changed so that they no longer function or dissolve.

A student who expects denaturation to reverse picks this. In fact denaturation is in most cases permanent: a cooked egg white does not become clear and liquid again when it cools, because the unfolded chains do not refold correctly.

This is denaturation. Heat makes the molecules vibrate more, breaking the bonds that maintain the three-dimensional shape; the unfolded chains tangle with one another, which is why the egg white becomes an insoluble solid.
questions.explain: This is denaturation. Heat makes the molecules vibrate more, breaking the bonds that maintain the three-dimensional shape; the unfolded chains tangle with one another, which is why the egg white becomes an insoluble solid.

questions.q: Which statement about the R-groups of amino acids is correct?
options: Every hydrophilic R-group must carry a charge; a polar R-group that is uncharged is classed as hydrophobic.
Hydrophilic R-groups are either polar but uncharged, or charged, and charged R-groups are acidic or basic.
An acidic R-group carries a positive charge, because an acid is a substance that contains hydrogen ions.
R-groups have little effect on a polypeptide, whose properties come from its amine and carboxyl groups.
optionWhy: A student who equates hydrophilic with charged picks this. In fact polar R-groups form hydrogen bonds with water and are hydrophilic even though they carry no overall charge; hydrophilic R-groups are polar or charged.

R-groups are hydrophobic or hydrophilic. Hydrophilic R-groups are polar or charged; a charged R-group is acidic if its carboxyl group has dissociated to become negative, or basic if its amine group has bound a hydrogen ion to become positive.

A student who links acid with H⁺ and so with positive charge picks this. In fact an acidic R-group releases its hydrogen ion and is left negatively charged; it is the basic R-group that binds a hydrogen ion and becomes positive.

A student who sees the fully drawn amine and carboxyl groups as the important chemistry picks this. In fact those groups are used up in peptide bonds to make a backbone common to all polypeptides; it is the R-groups that determine the properties of the assembled polypeptide.
questions.explain: R-groups are hydrophobic or hydrophilic. Hydrophilic R-groups are polar or charged; a charged R-group is acidic if its carboxyl group has dissociated to become negative, or basic if its amine group has bound a hydrogen ion to become positive.

questions.q: Thousands of copies of the same enzyme are synthesized in a cell, and every copy has the same three-dimensional shape. Why?
options: The ribosome and Golgi apparatus mould each polypeptide into the shape the cell needs after it has been synthesized.
Every copy contains the same set of amino acids, and the order in which they occur has no effect at all on the final shape.
The sequence of amino acids, each in its precise position, determines the conformation, so folding is repeatable.
Only the few amino acids that form the active site affect the shape, and these are the same in every copy.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a cell structure imposes the shape picks this. In fact the chain folds according to its own sequence; the ribosome joins the amino acids and the Golgi apparatus modifies proteins, but neither determines the conformation.

A student who treats a polypeptide as a mixture of ingredients picks this. In fact the shape depends on the sequence, not just the composition; the same amino acids in a different order would fold into a different shape.

The primary structure determines the three-dimensional shape: the R-groups in their exact positions can form only one set of bonds, so every polypeptide with that sequence folds the same way. Proteins therefore have precise, predictable and repeatable structures.

A student who sees the rest of the enzyme as filler picks this. In fact the precise position of every amino acid in the sequence contributes to the conformation, and the copies match because their whole sequences are identical.
questions.explain: The primary structure determines the three-dimensional shape: the R-groups in their exact positions can form only one set of bonds, so every polypeptide with that sequence folds the same way. Proteins therefore have precise, predictable and repeatable structures.

questions.q: What stabilizes the alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets of a protein's secondary structure?
options: Hydrogen bonds between the R-groups of amino acids brought close together by folding.
Disulfide bonds between cysteines spaced at regular intervals along the polypeptide.
Hydrogen bonds forming the peptide links between the amine and carboxyl groups of neighbours.
Hydrogen bonds at regular positions between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone.
optionWhy: A student who attaches every bond in a protein to R-groups picks this. In fact the R-groups project outwards from helices and sheets and take no part; the hydrogen bonds of secondary structure are between backbone groups.

A student who applies tertiary-structure bonding to secondary structure picks this. In fact disulfide bonds are between cysteine R-groups and belong to tertiary structure; helices and sheets depend on backbone hydrogen bonds.

A student who thinks peptide bonds are hydrogen bonds picks this. In fact peptide bonds are covalent and form the primary structure; the hydrogen bonds of secondary structure are additional, between the C=O and N–H groups of different peptide bonds.
Alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets are stabilized by hydrogen bonding in regular positions between the C=O group of one peptide bond and the N–H group of another in the polypeptide backbone.
questions.explain: Alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets are stabilized by hydrogen bonding in regular positions between the C=O group of one peptide bond and the N–H group of another in the polypeptide backbone.

questions.q: A globular enzyme is dissolved in the cytoplasm, and an integral protein spans the plasma membrane. Where are the amino acids with hydrophobic R-groups located in each protein, and why?
options: Absent from the soluble enzyme, because a protein containing hydrophobic amino acids could not dissolve in water.
Throughout the whole of the integral protein, which must be hydrophobic on all of its surfaces to stay in the membrane.
In the enzyme's core and the integral protein's membrane region, because water molecules bond to each other and exclude non-polar R-groups.
In the enzyme's core and the integral protein's membrane region, because their non-polar R-groups repel the water molecules and push them away.
optionWhy: A student who judges solubility by adding up the amino acids picks this. In fact soluble globular proteins do contain hydrophobic amino acids; they are clustered in the core, away from water, while the surface is hydrophilic.

A student who thinks anything in a membrane must be hydrophobic all over picks this. In fact only the region within the bilayer has hydrophobic R-groups; the parts projecting into the aqueous solutions on either side are hydrophilic.

In proteins that are soluble in water, hydrophobic amino acids are clustered in the core of the globular protein, and integral proteins have regions with hydrophobic amino acids that sit in the hydrophobic centre of the bilayer. They end up there because water molecules hydrogen-bond to one another and not to non-polar R-groups, which are therefore excluded from the water.

A student who pictures hydrophobic groups pushing water away picks this. The locations are right but the mechanism is not: there is no repulsion; water molecules bond to each other and exclude non-polar groups, so hydrophobic R-groups end up away from water.
questions.explain: In proteins that are soluble in water, hydrophobic amino acids are clustered in the core of the globular protein, and integral proteins have regions with hydrophobic amino acids that sit in the hydrophobic centre of the bilayer. They end up there because water molecules hydrogen-bond to one another and not to non-polar R-groups, which are therefore excluded from the water.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares insulin, collagen and haemoglobin?
options: All three are conjugated proteins, because each of them is built from more than one polypeptide chain.
The haem groups of haemoglobin are short polypeptides, so all three of these proteins are non-conjugated.
Insulin is a single polypeptide, so unlike collagen and haemoglobin it does not have quaternary structure.
Haemoglobin is a conjugated protein with haem groups; insulin and collagen are non-conjugated.
optionWhy: A student who thinks conjugated means multi-chain picks this. In fact all three have quaternary structure, but only haemoglobin is conjugated, because it contains non-polypeptide haem groups; insulin and collagen consist of polypeptides only.

A student who assumes everything in a protein is made of amino acids picks this. In fact a haem group is not a polypeptide: it is a ring structure containing an iron ion, and its presence is what makes haemoglobin a conjugated protein.

A student who assumes a small hormone must be a single chain picks this. In fact insulin consists of two polypeptides linked by disulfide bonds, so it has quaternary structure and is the guide's example of a non-conjugated protein.

Haemoglobin is conjugated because each of its four polypeptides carries a haem group, a prosthetic group not made of amino acids. Insulin (two polypeptides) and collagen (three polypeptides) have quaternary structure but no prosthetic group, so they are non-conjugated.
questions.explain: Haemoglobin is conjugated because each of its four polypeptides carries a haem group, a prosthetic group not made of amino acids. Insulin (two polypeptides) and collagen (three polypeptides) have quaternary structure but no prosthetic group, so they are non-conjugated.
